title: The prosecutor’s fallacy
objectives: Count the innocent matches in a pool to find the chance of guilt
Count the false discoveries when many strategies are tested

screens.prose: A stain at a crime scene matches the defendant’s DNA. The lab says an innocent person matches by chance 1 time in a million. The prosecutor tells the jury his chance of innocence is 1 in a million.

rows: People who could have left the stain

screens.question: Is the prosecutor’s figure about right?

options.text: No: it is far too low

options.why: The lab measured how often an innocent person matches. The jury needs how often a match is innocent, which is a different chance.

options.text: No: it is far too high
options.why: You sensed a problem but in the wrong direction. Count how many innocent people in the city would match by chance.

hints.text: How many people could have left the stain?
Apply the lab’s 1 in a million to everyone in the city.
5,000,000 people at 1 in a million each gives about 5 innocent matches, plus the culprit.

feedback.correct: The figure ignores how many innocent people would also match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the innocent matches you would expect in the city.

explain.text: With 5 million people, about 5 innocent people would match by chance. The defendant is one of about 6 people who match, not one in a million. We count them carefully next.

screens.prose: Suppose exactly one culprit, and nothing else to go on. Everyone in the pool is a suspect. Slide the size of the pool and watch how many innocent people match by chance.

derive.caption: Pool of {{fixed(N, 1)}} million: P(culprit | match) = {{fixed(1 / (1 + N), 3)}}

screens.question: Set the pool to 5 million. What is the chance that a person who matches is the culprit?

options.why: That is 1 minus the lab figure. It treats the lab’s 1 in a million as the chance of innocence.
You counted the 5 innocent matches but not the culprit. The culprit matches too, so there are about 6 matches.
Match or no match is not 50–50. Read the caption at 5 million.

hints.text: Count everyone who matches: the culprit and the innocent people.
At 5 million the innocent bar reaches 5.
About 6 people match and one is the culprit.

feedback.correct: One culprit among about six people who match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to 5 and read the caption.

explain.text: At 5 million the innocent bar is 5, beside the culprit’s 1. A match picks out one of about 6 people, so $P(\text{culprit} \mid \text{match}) \approx \tfrac{1}{6}$. The bigger the pool, the weaker the same match.

screens.prose: Here is the city as natural frequencies. One culprit, who matches for certain. The other 4,999,999 people each match with chance 1 in a million.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{innocent} \mid \text{match})$?

widget.label: Chance of innocence given a match

hints.text: Keep only the people who match.
Two branches end in a match.
About 6 people match and about 5 of them are innocent.

feedback.correct: About 5 of the 6 people who match are innocent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the innocent people among everyone who matches.

byKey.swap: That is the lab figure, $P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent})$. You need the condition the other way round: among the matches, how many are innocent?
byKey.guilty: That is the chance of guilt. The question asks for innocence.
byKey.prior: That is the chance of innocence before the test. Keep only the people who match.

explain.text: About 5 of the 6 matches are innocent: $P(\text{innocent} \mid \text{match}) \approx \tfrac{5}{6}$. The lab’s number was $P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent}) = 10^{-6}$. Swapping one for the other is the **prosecutor’s fallacy**.

screens.prose: Same match, new evidence. CCTV shows the culprit was one of 10 people locked in a building that night. The defendant is one of the 10.
screens.question: Now what is the chance that the defendant is the culprit, given the match?

options.why: You kept the whole city as the pool. The CCTV leaves only 10 people who could have done it.
That is the chance before the DNA test. The match is a million times likelier for the culprit than for anyone else.
Each innocent person can still match, with chance 1 in a million. Nine of them give about 0.000009 innocent matches.

hints.text: How many innocent people could match now?
Nine innocent people at 1 in a million each.
Innocent matches: about 0.000009. Culprit: 1. The chance is $\tfrac{1}{1.000009}$.

feedback.correct: Among 10 suspects, the same match is close to proof.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the count with 9 innocent people instead of 5 million.

explain.text: Prior odds of guilt are 1 to 9, and the match multiplies them by a million: about 111,111 to 1. So $P(\text{guilty} \mid \text{match}) \approx 0.99999$. The same lab result is weak in a city and overwhelming in a room of 10.

screens.prose: Back to the city of 5,000,000 with no other evidence. A better test cuts the chance of an innocent match to 1 in 10 million.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{guilty} \mid \text{match})$ now?

widget.label: Chance of guilt given a match

hints.text: How many innocent matches do you expect now?
5 million at 1 in 10 million each.
About 0.5 innocent matches and 1 culprit. The chance is $\tfrac{1}{1 + 0.5}$.

feedback.correct: One culprit against about half an innocent match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the expected innocent matches, then divide 1 by all the matches.

byKey.prosecutor: That is 1 minus the lab figure: the prosecutor’s fallacy again. Count the innocent matches.
byKey.old: That is the answer for the old 1-in-a-million test. The new test gives fewer innocent matches.
byKey.half-off: You divided the 0.5 innocent matches by 1. Divide the culprit’s 1 by all 1.5 matches.

explain.text: 5 million people at 1 in 10 million give about 0.5 innocent matches. So $P(\text{guilty} \mid \text{match}) = \tfrac{1}{1.5} = \tfrac{2}{3}$. The posterior depends on the pool size times the match rate, not on the match rate alone.

screens.prose: A newspaper reports the first trial: “DNA expert: only a one in a million chance he is innocent.” Look again at what the lab measured.
screens.question: What does the lab’s 1 in a million measure?

options.text: $P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent})$: how often an innocent person matches
$P(\text{innocent} \mid \text{match})$: how often a person who matches is innocent
options.why: You read the lab figure as the chance of innocence. That swaps the condition: among matches, about 5 in 6 are innocent.

options.text: $P(\text{innocent})$: the chance of innocence before the test
options.why: That chance is $\tfrac{4{,}999{,}999}{5{,}000{,}000}$, close to 1. The lab measured how often innocent people match.

options.text: $P(\text{match})$: the chance anyone in the city matches
options.why: That counts the culprit too, about 6 in 5 million. The lab tested innocent people only.

hints.text: Which group did the lab test to get its figure?
The lab’s figure lives on the branch from Innocent to Match.
The lab took innocent people and asked how often they match: match given innocent.

feedback.correct: The lab conditions on innocence; the jury needs to condition on the match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which group the lab’s figure is a share of.

byKey.swap: You quoted the match probability as the chance of innocence. The headline does the same: it swaps $P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent})$ for $P(\text{innocent} \mid \text{match})$.

explain.text: The lab’s figure is a share of innocent people: $P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent}) = 10^{-6}$. The headline needs a share of the people who match, about $\tfrac{5}{6}$ innocent. The two differ because innocent people vastly outnumber culprits.

screens.prose: Now the same answer in odds form, the way you would argue it in court. A guilty person always matches.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Prior odds of guilt $= \dfrac{1}{4{,}999{,}999}$: one culprit among 5 million people
Posterior odds $= \dfrac{1}{4{,}999{,}999} \times \dfrac{P(\text{match} \mid \text{guilty})}{P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent})}$, Bayes’ rule in odds form
$= \dfrac{1}{4{,}999{,}999} \times 10^{6} \approx 0.2$, since the culprit matches for certain

hints.text: Start with what we believe before the test.
The likelihood ratio multiplies the prior odds.
Prior odds, then Bayes’ rule, then put in the numbers, then convert to a probability.

feedback.correct: Prior odds times the likelihood ratio, then back to a probability.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the prior odds, then update them.

byKey.bayes: Bayes’ rule needs the prior odds first, so the prior line comes before it.
byKey.prob: The probability is read off the posterior odds, so it comes last.

explain.text: The likelihood ratio of $10^6$ is huge, but the prior odds of $1$ in $5$ million are tiny. Their product is about $0.2$, or $\tfrac{1}{6}$ as a probability. Strong evidence on a weak prior leaves a modest posterior.

screens.prose: A quant tests 1,000 trading strategies on the same price history. Suppose none of them has a real edge. A backtest p-value is $P(\text{a result at least this good} \mid \text{no edge})$.
screens.question: How many strategies do you expect to pass the test $p < 0.01$?

hints.text: Each strategy with no edge passes with chance 0.01.
All 1,000 have no edge.
Expected passes $= 1000 \times 0.01$.

feedback.correct: Ten strategies pass by luck alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number tested by the chance each passes by luck.

byKey.none: You read $p < 0.01$ as proof of an edge. A strategy with no edge still passes 1 time in 100.
byKey.one: That is 1 in 1,000. The chance of passing by luck is 1 in 100 for each strategy.

explain.text: $1000 \times 0.01 = 10$ strategies pass with no edge at all. Each of them has a p-value below 0.01. Test enough strategies and false discoveries are all but certain.

screens.prose: Now suppose 20 of the 1,000 strategies have a real edge, and a real edge passes the test with chance 0.5. One strategy passes.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{no edge} \mid \text{passes})$?

widget.label: Chance of no edge given a pass

hints.text: Keep only the strategies that pass.
Two branches end in a pass.
10 real edges and 9.8 lucky ones pass. The chance is $\tfrac{9.8}{19.8}$.

feedback.correct: About half of the passes are false discoveries.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Among the strategies that pass, find the share with no edge.

byKey.swap: That is the p-value threshold, $P(\text{pass} \mid \text{no edge})$. You need it the other way round.
byKey.prior: That is the share with no edge before testing. Keep only the passes.
byKey.edge: That is the chance of a real edge. The question asks for no edge.

explain.text: $\tfrac{9.8}{9.8 + 10} \approx 0.49$. A p-value of 0.01 is $P(\text{a result this good or better} \mid \text{no edge})$, not $P(\text{no edge} \mid \text{result})$. With few real edges among many tries, about half the discoveries are false.

ideas: $P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{innocent})$ and $P(\text{innocent} \mid \text{evidence})$ are different numbers. Swapping them is the prosecutor’s fallacy.
Turn a match rate into a count: pool size times the rate gives the innocent matches. The culprit is one of all the matches.
A p-value is the chance of a result at least this good, given no edge. Test many strategies and some pass by luck.

formula.name: Odds form
formula.note: A huge likelihood ratio can still leave a modest posterior when the prior odds are tiny.

summary.trap: Quoting the chance an innocent person matches as the chance a matching person is innocent.

quiz.prose: In the city of 5 million, the defence makes a claim. “The match leaves only a 1 in 6 chance of guilt. So the DNA evidence is worthless.”
quiz.question: What is wrong with the defence’s argument?

options.text: The match multiplied the odds of guilt by a million; it is strong evidence that needs other evidence beside it
Nothing: $\tfrac{1}{6}$ is weak, so the match can be ignored
options.why: Before the test he was one of 5 million. Moving to 1 in 6 is a huge update, not nothing.

options.text: The chance of guilt is really 999,999 in a million
options.why: That repeats the prosecutor’s fallacy. About 5 innocent people in the city match too.

feedback.correct: The match is strong evidence on a tiny prior.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the chance of guilt before and after the match.

explain.text: Before the match his chance of guilt was 1 in 5 million; after it, about $\tfrac{1}{6}$. That is a million-fold rise in the odds. Dismissing it is the defence’s mirror-image fallacy.

quiz.prose: A partial DNA profile matches an innocent person with chance 1 in 100,000. The stain could have come from any of 200,000 people, and nothing else points to the defendant.
quiz.question: What is the chance the matching defendant is the culprit?

widget.label: Chance of guilt given a match

feedback.correct: One culprit among about 3 people who match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the innocent matches in 200,000 people.

byKey.swap: That is 1 minus the match rate: the prosecutor’s fallacy. Count the innocent matches.
byKey.half: You split the matches 50–50 between guilty and innocent. There are 3 matches and 1 culprit.

explain.text: $200{,}000 \times \tfrac{1}{100{,}000} \approx 2$ innocent matches, plus the culprit: 3 in all. So $P(\text{guilty} \mid \text{match}) \approx \tfrac{1}{3}$.

quiz.prose: A screening test gives a positive result for 5% of healthy people.
quiz.question: Which statement says the same thing?

options.why: You swapped the condition. 5% is a share of healthy people, not a share of positives.
That would be a share of everyone tested. The 5% is a share of healthy people only.

feedback.correct: The 5% is a share of the healthy group.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which group the 5% is a share of.

explain.text: “Of healthy people, 5% test positive” conditions on being healthy: $P(\text{positive} \mid \text{healthy}) = 0.05$. The chance a positive is healthy needs the base rate as well.

quiz.prose: A researcher backtests 200 strategies, none with a real edge, and keeps every one with $p < 0.05$.
quiz.question: How many strategies does she expect to keep?

feedback.correct: Ten strategies are kept by luck alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number tested by 0.05.

byKey.none: Strategies with no edge still pass with chance 0.05 each.

explain.text: $200 \times 0.05 = 10$. Every one of them is a false discovery, and each has a p-value below 0.05.
